messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Threat

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Robert is a 72-year-old software engineer who, during a contract assignment in a conflict zone twenty years ago, was abducted by an armed group and held for six days. They interrogated him about the classified system he had helped design, and when he initially refused to cooperate, they subjected him to systematic torture—beating him, depriving him of sleep, water, and light, and forcing him to listen to the screams of other prisoners. On the fourth day, unable to endure any further, he gave them the access codes. The moment he spoke felt like a betrayal of everything he believed about himself. He had always prided himself on his integrity, and in that room he watched himself break. When he was finally released, he returned home physically unscathed but fundamentally altered.

Back in his small apartment—where he now lived alone after his marriage had ended years before—Robert found he could not shake the sense that he had become someone else, someone who had acted against his own values. He began to monitor his own thoughts with exhausting vigilance, scanning for any sign that he might be losing his grip, because part of him believed that a person who could do what he did must be going crazy. He tried hard not to think about the torture, pushing the memories away whenever they surfaced, but the effort only made him feel more alienated from himself and from the people around him. He had lost his faith in others; the faces he saw on the street seemed to him like masks, and he studied strangers’ expressions and body language with a practiced wariness, certain that danger could be hiding in plain sight. This constant threat monitoring fed directly into his negative appraisals: every time he caught someone’s gaze and saw nothing but threat, he felt more isolated, more convinced that no one could be trusted. He started checking the locks on his doors and windows repeatedly, sometimes three or four times before bed, and he struggled to fall asleep because his body remained alert for the sound of footsteps. These practices only deepened his sense of difference—other people did not live like this.

Robert had always worked as a remote software engineer, and for years that arrangement suited him. But after the torture, being alone in his apartment became intolerable. He began working from coffee shops and libraries, surrounded by strangers, yet still he felt set apart. He chose seating near exits so he could watch the door, and he tracked every person who entered. When a young man in a hoodie sat too close one afternoon, Robert’s heart pounded so hard he had to leave. He came to believe that his own vigilance was the only thing keeping him safe, but it also convinced him that the world was a hostile place—a belief that reinforced his loss of faith in people. His avoidance of solitude meant he spent hours in public spaces, but he rarely spoke to anyone, and his sense of isolation grew heavier. The more he suppressed thoughts of the trauma, the more they intruded, and the more he felt he was losing control of his mind, which only proved to him that he was indeed broken.

Now, at seventy-two, Robert has no close relationships. His adult daughter calls every Sunday, but she does not know the details of what happened, and he cannot bring himself to tell her. He recently found himself standing in front of his own bathroom mirror, studying his own face for signs of madness, and the absurdity of it startled him. That afternoon, for the first time, he searched online for help. What frightens him most is the possibility that he has already passed a point of no return—that the man who gave up the codes is the only person he really is now. He is hoping therapy can show him how to stop running from himself long enough to find out if there is anything left worth salvaging.
